PEPT1.logic: Proton-coupled oligopeptide transporter (SLC15A1) on the apical membrane of small-intestinal enterocytes. Although named for di- and tripeptides, its role in drug absorption is as a carrier-mediated uptake route for small-molecule drugs presenting a dipeptide-like scaffold. Its broad recognition of di-/tripeptide geometry is why chemically distinct classes are transported: beta-lactam antibiotics, ACE inhibitors, and amino-acid ester prodrugs. Molecules larger than a tripeptide are generally not transported.

Pgp.logic: ATP-binding cassette efflux transporter (ABCB1) on the apical membrane of enterocytes. It captures lipophilic and amphiphilic substrates from the membrane inner leaflet and extrudes them back into the lumen. Its transport capacity is finite and becomes saturated at the drug concentrations reached in the lumen after an ordinary oral dose, so it slows rather than prevents the net movement of a permeable molecule.

BCRP.logic: Homodimeric ATP-binding cassette efflux transporter (ABCG2) on the apical brush-border membrane. It preferentially effluxes planar aromatic and heterocyclic compounds and their sulfate and glucuronide conjugates. Like P-gp it is saturable and its substrate space overlaps with P-gp, and it opposes rather than abolishes the absorption of a passively permeable molecule.

CYP3A4.logic: The most abundant drug-metabolizing cytochrome P450 in enterocytes and liver, catalyzing oxidative metabolism of lipophilic substrates. It resides INSIDE the enterocyte and therefore acts only on drug that has already crossed the apical membrane. It lowers the fraction of absorbed drug reaching the circulation intact, which is a bioavailability effect occurring downstream of the absorption step this task asks about.

pathway_rules: HIA is the fraction of an orally administered dose that crosses the intestinal epithelium from the lumen into the enterocyte and the portal blood. It is distinct from systemic bioavailability, which additionally reflects first-pass metabolism in the gut wall and liver acting on drug that has already been absorbed.

PEPT1 (SLC15A1) is a proton-coupled oligopeptide transporter on the apical membrane of small-intestinal enterocytes. It mediates carrier-mediated influx of di- and tripeptides and of peptidomimetic drugs sharing that scaffold, including beta-lactam antibiotics, ACE inhibitors, and amino-acid ester prodrugs; molecules larger than a tripeptide are not transported.

P-glycoprotein (ABCB1) is an ATP-driven efflux transporter on the apical membrane of enterocytes. It binds lipophilic and amphiphilic substrates within the inner leaflet of the membrane and extrudes them back into the intestinal lumen. Its transport capacity is finite and becomes saturated at the luminal drug concentrations reached after an ordinary oral dose.

BCRP (ABCG2) is a homodimeric ATP-driven efflux transporter on the apical brush-border membrane of enterocytes. It preferentially extrudes planar aromatic and heterocyclic compounds and their sulfate and glucuronide conjugates. Its substrate specificity overlaps with that of P-glycoprotein, and like P-glycoprotein it is saturable at luminal concentrations.

CYP3A4 is the most abundant drug-metabolizing cytochrome P450 in enterocytes and hepatocytes and catalyzes oxidative Phase I metabolism of lipophilic substrates. It is located intracellularly and acts only on drug that has already crossed the apical membrane, contributing to gut-wall and hepatic first-pass metabolism downstream of the absorption step.

yes_features: Beta-lactam ring (penicillin, cephalosporin, carbapenem scaffold): recognized by PEPT1 as a dipeptide mimic through its amide carbonyl and nitrogen H-bond geometry, giving carrier-mediated apical uptake even when passive permeability is low.

Free alpha-amino-acid backbone, or an amino-acid ester appended to a polar scaffold: recognized by PEPT1 through its di-/tripeptide-like geometry, the basis of amino-acid ester prodrugs that gain carrier-mediated apical uptake.

Short-chain aliphatic monocarboxylate (C1-C4 acid without bulky or additional ionizable substituents): its small size and the neutral fraction present at intestinal pH permit passive transcellular and paracellular absorption.

Small neutral molecule (molecular weight below ~250) with TPSA below ~80 A^2 and no permanently charged centre: absorbed efficiently by transcellular diffusion and by the paracellular route, regardless of low lipophilicity.
Neutral scaffold carrying no more than one hydrogen-bond donor with TPSA below ~90 A^2: the low desolvation cost permits efficient partitioning into the apical membrane even at low or negative logP.

N-methylated amide bonds in cyclic or macrocyclic peptides: removing hydrogen-bond-donor NH groups raises passive membrane permeability without adding lipophilicity, enabling absorption of some large macrocyclic peptides.
no_features: Permanent quaternary ammonium (fixed positive charge at all physiological pH): no neutral fraction exists, precluding passive transcellular diffusion and peptide-transporter recognition.
Geminal bisphosphonate group (multiple ionizable phosphonate protons): heavily anionic across intestinal pH and strongly hydrated, blocking both passive diffusion and carrier recognition.
Aminoglycoside-like scaffold: two or more glycosidic linkages bearing multiple free amino and hydroxyl groups, giving a large hydrated polar surface that cannot partition into the apical membrane.

Peptide backbone of four or more residues with free, non-N-methylated amide NH groups: too large for PEPT1, which is limited to di- and tripeptide geometry, and carrying too many hydrogen-bond donors for passive permeability.

TPSA above ~140 A^2 together with more than 5 hydrogen-bond donors: the combined desolvation penalty is too large for the passive transcellular route, and the molecule is also too polar for membrane partitioning.

logP above ~5 combined with molecular weight above ~600: dissolution in intestinal fluid becomes the limiting step, so little drug is available in solution to be absorbed despite a membrane-permeable scaffold.
